rv.q: And yet this sensually shocking and impeccably acted production—a high point in my years attending the Roundabout—feels stingingly fresh and provocative.

Indeed, the play is so rigorously brutal and swift it almost gets to the end before you realize that the expressionism is a bit of a smoke screen, the alterations to the Snyder story a bit of a dodge.

Machinal remains perhaps too defined by theatrical artifice and pre-feminist theory to be as shattering as the events it depicts, but it merits attention as a bold excursion beyond standard Broadway fare.

But Hall -- with a beanpole body like an exclamation point and a face of a thousand worried looks -- brings us deep inside the long, virtuosic bursts of halting half-sentences and tangled mazes of internal monologues.
The result at the Theatre is a quirky, sometimes melodramatic and expressionist scream from the past that somehow still can move you.
Ms. Pill gives what may well be the performance of her career, portraying Helen as a woman whose inability to connect with other people ultimately drives her to murder.
That slackness has the unfortunate side effect of making Ms. Hall’s character seem less a sensitive victim of a brute society than of her own mental illness.
But it’s tough to empathize with someone who lacks a backbone and hasn’t a brain in her head.
Lyndsey Turner’s extraordinary production makes for an absolutely stirring 90 minutes of theater.
But if you're up for an intense theatrical experience, this one's a first-class punch to the gut.
The unravelling of Hall’s tormented psyche is gripping.
Thanks to Hall's haunted characterization, though, the essence of the play, the sense of an individual plowed over by the inexorable surge of society, never fades.
Unfortunately, Machinal isn’t consistently intriguing or the tiniest bit emotionally involving.
By the time Machinal runs its course, theatergoers may feel as if they're the ones who have been beaten into submission, by an anti-heroine who inspires dark fascination but little empathy.
Treadwell's play is stylish but slight.
I just didn’t like Helen very much, so her death never felt like a terrible loss.
This may be the best-staged play of the season, certainly one of the most aptly designed.
Nearly a century later, the shock may be the play's continued relevance.
What you take home is the intensity of the tale.
The noirish dialogue is based on unrelenting repetitions and the didactic clichés of the era.
